claim: PMA induces neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) in primary human neutrophils.
source: Primary human neutrophils were stimulated for the indicated times with 50 nM PMA, 5 µM A23187, 15 µM nigericin, MOI 5 opsonized C. albicans or MOI 10 opsonized group B streptococcus (GBS), fixed with 2% PFA and incubated with a DNA stain (Hoechst) and immunolabeled with antibodies directed against Neutrophil Elastase (NE) and chromatin (A–G). (A) NETosis rate was quantified by immunofluorescence.
evidence: Experimental data showing NET formation quantified by immunofluorescence in response to PMA stimulation (Figure 1A).

claim: A23187 induces neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) in primary human neutrophils.
source: Primary human neutrophils were stimulated for the indicated times with 50 nM PMA, 5 µM A23187, 15 µM nigericin, MOI 5 opsonized C. albicans or MOI 10 opsonized group B streptococcus (GBS), fixed with 2% PFA and incubated with a DNA stain (Hoechst) and immunolabeled with antibodies directed against Neutrophil Elastase (NE) and chromatin (A–G). (A) NETosis rate was quantified by immunofluorescence.
evidence: Experimental data showing NET formation quantified by immunofluorescence in response to A23187 stimulation (Figure 1A).

claim: Nigericin induces neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) in primary human neutrophils.
source: Primary human neutrophils were stimulated for the indicated times with 50 nM PMA, 5 µM A23187, 15 µM nigericin, MOI 5 opsonized C. albicans or MOI 10 opsonized group B streptococcus (GBS), fixed with 2% PFA and incubated with a DNA stain (Hoechst) and immunolabeled with antibodies directed against Neutrophil Elastase (NE) and chromatin (A–G). (A) NETosis rate was quantified by immunofluorescence.
evidence: Experimental data showing NET formation quantified by immunofluorescence in response to nigericin stimulation (Figure 1A).

claim: Candida albicans induces neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) in primary human neutrophils.
source: Primary human neutrophils were stimulated for the indicated times with 50 nM PMA, 5 µM A23187, 15 µM nigericin, MOI 5 opsonized C. albicans or MOI 10 opsonized group B streptococcus (GBS), fixed with 2% PFA and incubated with a DNA stain (Hoechst) and immunolabeled with antibodies directed against Neutrophil Elastase (NE) and chromatin (A–G). (A) NETosis rate was quantified by immunofluorescence.
evidence: Experimental data showing NET formation quantified by immunofluorescence in response to C. albicans stimulation (Figure 1A).

claim: Group B Streptococcus (GBS) induces neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) in primary human neutrophils.
source: Primary human neutrophils were stimulated for the indicated times with 50 nM PMA, 5 µM A23187, 15 µM nigericin, MOI 5 opsonized C. albicans or MOI 10 opsonized group B streptococcus (GBS), fixed with 2% PFA and incubated with a DNA stain (Hoechst) and immunolabeled with antibodies directed against Neutrophil Elastase (NE) and chromatin (A–G). (A) NETosis rate was quantified by immunofluorescence.
evidence: Experimental data showing NET formation quantified by immunofluorescence in response to GBS stimulation (Figure 1A).

claim: NETs induced by all five stimuli contain extracellular DNA co-localized with neutrophil elastase and chromatin.
source: Activating neutrophils with each of the stimuli resulted in a similar NET structure containing extracellular DNA co-localised with NE and chromatin (Figure 1B–G).
evidence: Confocal microscopy images showing co-localization of DNA, NE, and chromatin in NETs induced by all five stimuli (Figure 1B-G).

claim: PMA-induced NET formation is blocked by the PKC inhibitor Gö6976.
source: As anticipated, PMA-induced NET formation was blocked by the PKC inhibitor Gö6976 (Figure 2A) (Gray et al., 2013).
evidence: Experimental data showing inhibition of PMA-induced NETosis by PKC inhibitor (Figure 2A), supported by citation to Gray et al., 2013.

claim: C. albicans-induced NET formation is blocked by the PKC inhibitor Gö6976.
source: C. albicans and GBS NET induction was also blocked by the PKC inhibitor, albeit to a lesser degree (Figure 2C).
evidence: Experimental data showing partial inhibition of C. albicans-induced NETosis by PKC inhibitor (Figure 2C).

claim: GBS-induced NET formation is blocked by the PKC inhibitor Gö6976.
source: C. albicans and GBS NET induction was also blocked by the PKC inhibitor, albeit to a lesser degree (Figure 2C).
evidence: Experimental data showing partial inhibition of GBS-induced NETosis by PKC inhibitor (Figure 2C).

claim: A23187-induced NET formation does not require PKC.
source: The two ionophores, conversely, did not require PKC (Figure 2B).
evidence: Experimental data showing no effect of PKC inhibitor on A23187-induced NETosis (Figure 2B).

claim: Nigericin-induced NET formation does not require PKC.
source: The two ionophores, conversely, did not require PKC (Figure 2B).
evidence: Experimental data showing no effect of PKC inhibitor on nigericin-induced NETosis (Figure 2B).

claim: PMA-induced NETosis is impaired by the calcium chelator BAPTA-AM.
source: PMA (Figure 2D) and nigericin (Figure 2E), induced NETosis was impaired by the calcium chelator BAPTA-AM.
evidence: Experimental data showing inhibition of PMA-induced NETosis by calcium chelator (Figure 2D).

claim: Nigericin-induced NETosis is impaired by the calcium chelator BAPTA-AM.
source: PMA (Figure 2D) and nigericin (Figure 2E), induced NETosis was impaired by the calcium chelator BAPTA-AM.
evidence: Experimental data showing inhibition of nigericin-induced NETosis by calcium chelator (Figure 2E).

claim: A23187-induced NETosis is only slightly reduced by the calcium chelator BAPTA-AM.
source: This chelator reduced NET formation only slightly in response to A23187 (Figure 2E).
evidence: Experimental data showing minimal effect of calcium chelator on A23187-induced NETosis (Figure 2E).

claim: Calcium chelation does not impair C. albicans-induced NETosis.
source: Notably, calcium chelation did not impair NETosis in response to C. albicans or GBS (Figure 2F).
evidence: Experimental data showing no effect of calcium chelator on C. albicans-induced NETosis (Figure 2F).

claim: Calcium chelation does not impair GBS-induced NETosis.
source: Notably, calcium chelation did not impair NETosis in response to C. albicans or GBS (Figure 2F).
evidence: Experimental data showing no effect of calcium chelator on GBS-induced NETosis (Figure 2F).

claim: PMA-induced NET formation is independent of transcription.
source: Finally, as previously shown for PMA and C. albicans, A23187, nigericin and GBS NET induction is independent of transcription (Figure 2G–I) (Sollberger et al., 2016).
evidence: Experimental data showing no effect of actinomycin D on PMA-induced NETosis (Figure 2G), supported by citation to Sollberger et al., 2016.

claim: A23187-induced NET formation is independent of transcription.
source: Finally, as previously shown for PMA and C. albicans, A23187, nigericin and GBS NET induction is independent of transcription (Figure 2G–I) (Sollberger et al., 2016).
evidence: Experimental data showing no effect of actinomycin D on A23187-induced NETosis (Figure 2H).

claim: Nigericin-induced NET formation is independent of transcription.
source: Finally, as previously shown for PMA and C. albicans, A23187, nigericin and GBS NET induction is independent of transcription (Figure 2G–I) (Sollberger et al., 2016).
evidence: Experimental data showing no effect of actinomycin D on nigericin-induced NETosis (Figure 2H).

claim: C. albicans-induced NET formation is independent of transcription.
source: Finally, as previously shown for PMA and C. albicans, A23187, nigericin and GBS NET induction is independent of transcription (Figure 2G–I) (Sollberger et al., 2016).
evidence: Experimental data showing no effect of actinomycin D on C. albicans-induced NETosis (Figure 2I), supported by citation to Sollberger et al., 2016.

claim: GBS-induced NET formation is independent of transcription.
source: Finally, as previously shown for PMA and C. albicans, A23187, nigericin and GBS NET induction is independent of transcription (Figure 2G–I) (Sollberger et al., 2016).
evidence: Experimental data showing no effect of actinomycin D on GBS-induced NETosis (Figure 2I).

claim: PMA induces a ROS burst in primary human neutrophils that peaks after 20 minutes of stimulation.
source: Figure 3A confirms that PMA induced a ROS burst in primary human neutrophils, peaking after 20 min of stimulation.
evidence: Experimental data showing ROS production kinetics in response to PMA (Figure 3A).

claim: The PMA-induced ROS burst is largely abolished by pre-treating neutrophils with the ROS scavenger pyrocatechol.
source: This ROS burst was largely abolished by pre-treating the neutrophils with the ROS scavenger pyrocatechol.
evidence: Experimental data showing inhibition of PMA-induced ROS by pyrocatechol (Figure 3A).

claim: A23187 induces a ROS burst with slower kinetics than PMA, peaking around 80 minutes post stimulation.
source: A23187 (Figure 3B) also induced a ROS burst, although with slower kinetics than PMA, peaking around 80 min post stimulation.
evidence: Experimental data showing ROS production kinetics in response to A23187 (Figure 3B).

claim: Pyrocatechol prevents the A23187-induced ROS burst.
source: Pyrocatechol also prevented this ROS burst.
evidence: Experimental data showing inhibition of A23187-induced ROS by pyrocatechol (Figure 3B).

claim: Nigericin does not induce ROS production.
source: In contrast, nigericin did not induce any ROS production (Figure 3B).
evidence: Experimental data showing no ROS production in response to nigericin (Figure 3B).

claim: Opsonized C. albicans generates ROS that peaks 20 minutes after activation.
source: Opsonized C. albicans generated ROS (Figure 3C) peaked, like PMA 20 min after activation.
evidence: Experimental data showing ROS production kinetics in response to C. albicans (Figure 3C).

claim: GBS induces ROS production to similar levels as C. albicans but with slower kinetics.
source: GBS-induced ROS production to similar levels but with slower kinetics.
evidence: Experimental data showing ROS production kinetics in response to GBS (Figure 3C).

claim: ROS release by C. albicans and GBS is abrogated by pyrocatechol.
source: ROS release by both microbes was abrogated by pyrocatechol.
evidence: Experimental data showing inhibition of C. albicans and GBS-induced ROS by pyrocatechol (Figure 3C).

claim: ROS is absolutely required for PMA-induced NETosis.
source: As expected, ROS was absolutely required for PMA-induced NETosis (Figure 3D).
evidence: Experimental data showing complete inhibition of PMA-induced NETosis by ROS scavenger (Figure 3D).

claim: Pyrocatechol does not affect the level of NETosis in response to A23187.
source: Conversely, pyrocatechol did not affect the level of NETosis in response to A23187 or nigericin (Figure 3E).
evidence: Experimental data showing no effect of ROS scavenger on A23187-induced NETosis (Figure 3E).

claim: Pyrocatechol does not affect the level of NETosis in response to nigericin.
source: Conversely, pyrocatechol did not affect the level of NETosis in response to A23187 or nigericin (Figure 3E).
evidence: Experimental data showing no effect of ROS scavenger on nigericin-induced NETosis (Figure 3E).

claim: C. albicans-induced NETosis is impaired in the presence of the ROS scavenger pyrocatechol.
source: Interestingly, C. albicans-induced NETosis was impaired in the presence of the ROS scavenger, but GBS-induced NETosis was not (Figure 3F).
evidence: Experimental data showing inhibition of C. albicans-induced NETosis by ROS scavenger (Figure 3F).

claim: GBS-induced NETosis is not impaired in the presence of the ROS scavenger pyrocatechol.
source: Interestingly, C. albicans-induced NETosis was impaired in the presence of the ROS scavenger, but GBS-induced NETosis was not (Figure 3F).
evidence: Experimental data showing no effect of ROS scavenger on GBS-induced NETosis (Figure 3F).

claim: Neutrophils from CGD patients are deficient in ROS production.
source: As expected, the neutrophils from these patients were deficient in ROS production (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Experimental data showing lack of ROS production in CGD patient neutrophils (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).

claim: CGD patient neutrophils do not undergo NETosis in response to PMA.
source: As previously described (Fuchs et al., 2007), CGD patient neutrophils did not undergo NETosis in response to PMA (Figure 3G) and were also significantly impaired in NET production in the presence of S. aureus (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Experimental data showing lack of PMA-induced NETosis in CGD patient neutrophils (Figure 3G), supported by citation to Fuchs et al., 2007.

claim: CGD patient neutrophils are significantly impaired in NET production in the presence of S. aureus.
source: As previously described (Fuchs et al., 2007), CGD patient neutrophils did not undergo NETosis in response to PMA (Figure 3G) and were also significantly impaired in NET production in the presence of S. aureus (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Experimental data showing impaired S. aureus-induced NETosis in CGD patient neutrophils (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).

claim: A23187 does not require ROS to generate NETs.
source: Notably, and confirming our data with the ROS scavenger, neither A23187 nor nigericin required ROS to generate NETs (Figure 3H).
evidence: Experimental data showing normal A23187-induced NETosis in CGD patient neutrophils (Figure 3H).

claim: Nigericin does not require ROS to generate NETs.
source: Notably, and confirming our data with the ROS scavenger, neither A23187 nor nigericin required ROS to generate NETs (Figure 3H).
evidence: Experimental data showing normal nigericin-induced NETosis in CGD patient neutrophils (Figure 3H).

claim: There is no significant difference in the levels of NETosis comparing healthy vs. CGD patient neutrophils in response to C. albicans.
source: Intriguingly, and in contrast to data obtained with the ROS scavenger, there was no significant difference in the levels of NETosis comparing healthy vs. CGD patient neutrophils in response to C. albicans.
evidence: Experimental data comparing C. albicans-induced NETosis in healthy and CGD patient neutrophils (Figure 3I).

claim: C. albicans can induce a ROS burst itself in the absence of neutrophils.
source: This discrepancy was explained by the fact that C. albicans can induce a ROS burst itself in the absence of neutrophils and this was inhibited in the presence of the ROS scavenger pyrocatechol (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Experimental data showing ROS production by C. albicans alone (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).

claim: C. albicans produces sufficient ROS to allow NETosis in CGD patient neutrophils.
source: Indeed, we confirmed that C. albicans produces sufficient ROS to allow NETosis.
evidence: Experimental data showing that pre-treating C. albicans with pyrocatechol inhibits NETosis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Scavenging C. albicans-derived ROS inhibits NET production.
source: We pre-incubated the fungus with pyrocatechol (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) and showed that scavenging C. albicans-derived ROS also inhibited NET production.
evidence: Experimental data showing inhibition of NETosis when C. albicans is pre-treated with pyrocatechol (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).

claim: The amount of NETs produced by GBS is decreased in CGD neutrophils when compared with cells isolated from healthy donors.
source: Moreover, by inhibiting ROS in both the neutrophils and the fungus NETosis was inhibited to a greater extent. Thus, the amount of ROS produced by the C. albicans was sufficient to allow NETs induction in CGD neutrophils. The amount of NETs were, however, decreased in CGD neutrophils infected with GBS (Figure 3I) when compared with cells isolated from healthy donors.
evidence: Experimental data showing decreased GBS-induced NETosis in CGD patient neutrophils (Figure 3I).

claim: ROS generated by the NADPH oxidase is absolutely essential for PMA-induced NETosis.
source: Overall, these data show that ROS generated by the NADPH oxidase, while absolutely essential for PMA-induced NETosis, are not necessary for NET production in response to both ionophores and only partially required for C. albicans and GBS-induced NETosis.
evidence: Summary of experimental data from ROS scavenger and CGD patient experiments.

claim: ROS generated by the NADPH oxidase is not necessary for NET production in response to ionophores.
source: Overall, these data show that ROS generated by the NADPH oxidase, while absolutely essential for PMA-induced NETosis, are not necessary for NET production in response to both ionophores and only partially required for C. albicans and GBS-induced NETosis.
evidence: Summary of experimental data from ROS scavenger and CGD patient experiments.

claim: ROS generated by the NADPH oxidase is only partially required for C. albicans-induced NETosis.
source: Overall, these data show that ROS generated by the NADPH oxidase, while absolutely essential for PMA-induced NETosis, are not necessary for NET production in response to both ionophores and only partially required for C. albicans and GBS-induced NETosis.
evidence: Summary of experimental data from ROS scavenger and CGD patient experiments.

claim: ROS generated by the NADPH oxidase is only partially required for GBS-induced NETosis.
source: Overall, these data show that ROS generated by the NADPH oxidase, while absolutely essential for PMA-induced NETosis, are not necessary for NET production in response to both ionophores and only partially required for C. albicans and GBS-induced NETosis.
evidence: Summary of experimental data from ROS scavenger and CGD patient experiments.

claim: Pre-treatment of neutrophils with ABAH significantly decreases PMA-induced NET formation.
source: Pre-treatment of neutrophils with ABAH did not induce spontaneous NETosis and, as anticipated, significantly decreased PMA-induced NET formation (Figure 4A).
evidence: Experimental data showing inhibition of PMA-induced NETosis by MPO inhibitor ABAH (Figure 4A).

claim: Neutrophils from a MPO-deficient patient show decreased PMA-induced NET formation.
source: This was confirmed with neutrophils isolated from a MPO-deficient patient stimulated with PMA (Figure 4D).
evidence: Experimental data showing impaired PMA-induced NETosis in MPO-deficient patient neutrophils (Figure 4D).

claim: The MPO inhibitor ABAH does not affect NET production by A23187.
source: Similar to the lack of ROS requirement in NETosis in response to ionophores, the MPO inhibitor did not affect NET production by A23187 or nigericin (Figure 4B) and neutrophils from a MPO-deficient individual underwent NETosis in response to both stimuli (Figure 4E).
evidence: Experimental data showing no effect of MPO inhibitor on A23187-induced NETosis (Figure 4B).

claim: The MPO inhibitor ABAH does not affect NET production by nigericin.
source: Similar to the lack of ROS requirement in NETosis in response to ionophores, the MPO inhibitor did not affect NET production by A23187 or nigericin (Figure 4B) and neutrophils from a MPO-deficient individual underwent NETosis in response to both stimuli (Figure 4E).
evidence: Experimental data showing no effect of MPO inhibitor on nigericin-induced NETosis (Figure 4B).

claim: Neutrophils from a MPO-deficient individual undergo NETosis in response to A23187.
source: Similar to the lack of ROS requirement in NETosis in response to ionophores, the MPO inhibitor did not affect NET production by A23187 or nigericin (Figure 4B) and neutrophils from a MPO-deficient individual underwent NETosis in response to both stimuli (Figure 4E).
evidence: Experimental data showing normal A23187-induced NETosis in MPO-deficient patient neutrophils (Figure 4E).

claim: Neutrophils from a MPO-deficient individual undergo NETosis in response to nigericin.
source: Similar to the lack of ROS requirement in NETosis in response to ionophores, the MPO inhibitor did not affect NET production by A23187 or nigericin (Figure 4B) and neutrophils from a MPO-deficient individual underwent NETosis in response to both stimuli (Figure 4E).
evidence: Experimental data showing normal nigericin-induced NETosis in MPO-deficient patient neutrophils (Figure 4E).

claim: NETs induced by C. albicans require MPO.
source: Interestingly, and contrary to the subtle role of ROS in NETosis induction, NETs induced by C. albicans or GBS stimulation required MPO (Figure 4C and F).
evidence: Experimental data showing inhibition of C. albicans-induced NETosis by MPO inhibitor and in MPO-deficient patient neutrophils (Figure 4C and F).

claim: NETs induced by GBS require MPO.
source: Interestingly, and contrary to the subtle role of ROS in NETosis induction, NETs induced by C. albicans or GBS stimulation required MPO (Figure 4C and F).
evidence: Experimental data showing inhibition of GBS-induced NETosis by MPO inhibitor and in MPO-deficient patient neutrophils (Figure 4C and F).

claim: Pre-treatment of healthy neutrophils with a neutrophil elastase inhibitor significantly impairs PMA-induced NETs.
source: Pre-treatment of healthy neutrophils with a highly specific small molecule NE inhibitor (Macdonald et al., 2001) did not result in spontaneous NETosis and significantly impaired PMA, C. albicans and GBS induced NETs (Figure 5A and C).
evidence: Experimental data showing inhibition of PMA-induced NETosis by NE inhibitor (Figure 5A), supported by citation to Macdonald et al., 2001.

claim: Pre-treatment of healthy neutrophils with a neutrophil elastase inhibitor significantly impairs C. albicans-induced NETs.
source: Pre-treatment of healthy neutrophils with a highly specific small molecule NE inhibitor (Macdonald et al., 2001) did not result in spontaneous NETosis and significantly impaired PMA, C. albicans and GBS induced NETs (Figure 5A and C).
evidence: Experimental data showing inhibition of C. albicans-induced NETosis by NE inhibitor (Figure 5C).

claim: Pre-treatment of healthy neutrophils with a neutrophil elastase inhibitor significantly impairs GBS-induced NETs.
source: Pre-treatment of healthy neutrophils with a highly specific small molecule NE inhibitor (Macdonald et al., 2001) did not result in spontaneous NETosis and significantly impaired PMA, C. albicans and GBS induced NETs (Figure 5A and C).
evidence: Experimental data showing inhibition of GBS-induced NETosis by NE inhibitor (Figure 5C).

claim: NETosis in response to A23187 does not require neutrophil elastase.
source: NETosis in response to A23187 and nigericin did not require NE (Figure 5B).
evidence: Experimental data showing no effect of NE inhibitor on A23187-induced NETosis (Figure 5B).

claim: NETosis in response to nigericin does not require neutrophil elastase.
source: NETosis in response to A23187 and nigericin did not require NE (Figure 5B).
evidence: Experimental data showing no effect of NE inhibitor on nigericin-induced NETosis (Figure 5B).

claim: Stimulation of neutrophils with A23187 results in Histone H3 citrullination within 90 minutes.
source: Stimulation of neutrophils with A23187, nigericin, C. albicans and GBS, but not PMA, resulted in Histone H3 citrullination (cit-H3) within 90 min as shown by Western blot analysis, (Figure 6A) confirming previous publications for both PMA and the calcium ionophore (Neeli and Radic, 2013).
evidence: Western blot data showing citrullinated histone H3 in response to A23187 (Figure 6A), supported by citation to Neeli and Radic, 2013.

claim: Stimulation of neutrophils with nigericin results in Histone H3 citrullination within 90 minutes.
source: Stimulation of neutrophils with A23187, nigericin, C. albicans and GBS, but not PMA, resulted in Histone H3 citrullination (cit-H3) within 90 min as shown by Western blot analysis, (Figure 6A) confirming previous publications for both PMA and the calcium ionophore (Neeli and Radic, 2013).
evidence: Western blot data showing citrullinated histone H3 in response to nigericin (Figure 6A).

claim: Stimulation of neutrophils with C. albicans results in Histone H3 citrullination within 90 minutes.
source: Stimulation of neutrophils with A23187, nigericin, C. albicans and GBS, but not PMA, resulted in Histone H3 citrullination (cit-H3) within 90 min as shown by Western blot analysis, (Figure 6A) confirming previous publications for both PMA and the calcium ionophore (Neeli and Radic, 2013).
evidence: Western blot data showing citrullinated histone H3 in response to C. albicans (Figure 6A).

claim: Stimulation of neutrophils with GBS results in Histone H3 citrullination within 90 minutes.
source: Stimulation of neutrophils with A23187, nigericin, C. albicans and GBS, but not PMA, resulted in Histone H3 citrullination (cit-H3) within 90 min as shown by Western blot analysis, (Figure 6A) confirming previous publications for both PMA and the calcium ionophore (Neeli and Radic, 2013).
evidence: Western blot data showing citrullinated histone H3 in response to GBS (Figure 6A).

claim: Stimulation of neutrophils with PMA does not result in Histone H3 citrullination within 90 minutes.
source: Stimulation of neutrophils with A23187, nigericin, C. albicans and GBS, but not PMA, resulted in Histone H3 citrullination (cit-H3) within 90 min as shown by Western blot analysis, (Figure 6A) confirming previous publications for both PMA and the calcium ionophore (Neeli and Radic, 2013).
evidence: Western blot data showing no citrullinated histone H3 in response to PMA (Figure 6A), supported by citation to Neeli and Radic, 2013.

claim: Very few of the PMA induced NETs stain positively for citrullinated histone H3.
source: Very few of the PMA induced NETs (Figure 6B) stained positively for cit-H3.
evidence: Immunofluorescence data showing minimal cit-H3 staining in PMA-induced NETs (Figure 6B).

claim: PMA-induced NETosis is not affected by PAD inhibitors Cl-amidine, BB-Cl-amidine, or TDFA.
source: Treating neutrophils with Cl-amidine, BB-Cl-amidine or TDFA did not induce NETosis spontaneously (Figure 6E). PMA induced NETosis was not affected by these inhibitors, consistent with the data obtained with GSK199, another PAD4-selective inhibitor (Figure 6E) (Lewis et al., 2015).
evidence: Experimental data showing no effect of PAD inhibitors on PMA-induced NETosis (Figure 6E), supported by citation to Lewis et al., 2015.

claim: A23187-induced NETosis remains intact after incubation with PAD inhibitors Cl-amidine, BB-Cl-amidine, or TDFA.
source: Importantly, in response to A23187 or nigericin stimulation, NETosis remained intact after incubation with the three inhibitors (Figure 6F).
evidence: Experimental data showing no effect of PAD inhibitors on A23187-induced NETosis (Figure 6F).

claim: Nigericin-induced NETosis remains intact after incubation with PAD inhibitors Cl-amidine, BB-Cl-amidine, or TDFA.
source: Importantly, in response to A23187 or nigericin stimulation, NETosis remained intact after incubation with the three inhibitors (Figure 6F).
evidence: Experimental data showing no effect of PAD inhibitors on nigericin-induced NETosis (Figure 6F).

claim: C. albicans-induced NETosis is not affected by PAD inhibitors Cl-amidine, BB-Cl-amidine, or TDFA.
source: Similarly, these inhibitors did not affect C. albicans or GBS-induced NETosis (Figure 6G).
evidence: Experimental data showing no effect of PAD inhibitors on C. albicans-induced NETosis (Figure 6G).

claim: GBS-induced NETosis is not affected by PAD inhibitors Cl-amidine, BB-Cl-amidine, or TDFA.
source: Similarly, these inhibitors did not affect C. albicans or GBS-induced NETosis (Figure 6G).
evidence: Experimental data showing no effect of PAD inhibitors on GBS-induced NETosis (Figure 6G).

claim: Histone H3 citrullination occurs during NETosis in response to A23187, nigericin, C. albicans and GBS but not PMA.
source: These data show that histone H3 citrullination occurs during the course of NETosis in response to A23187, nigericin, C. albicans and GBS but not PMA-induced NETs.
evidence: Summary of Western blot and immunofluorescence data on histone H3 citrullination.

claim: PAD2 and PAD4 are not required for NETosis.
source: Moreover, the inhibitor assays demonstrate that PAD2 and PAD4 are not required for NETosis.
evidence: Summary of experimental data using PAD inhibitors showing no effect on NETosis.

claim: Induction of NETosis with all five stimuli results in the degradation of histone H3 at both 90 and 180 minutes.
source: As previously shown for PMA (Papayannopoulos et al., 2010), the induction of NETosis with all five stimuli resulted in the degradation of histone H3 at both 90 and 180 min (Figure 7A).
evidence: Western blot data showing histone H3 degradation in response to all five stimuli (Figure 7A), supported by citation to Papayannopoulos et al., 2010.

claim: NETs from all five stimuli are capable of degrading FITC-labelled casein to a similar level.
source: This was further confirmed by assaying the degradation of FITC-labelled casein in the presence of NETs isolated from healthy neutrophils treated with the five stimuli (Figure 7B). NETs from all five stimuli were capable of degrading FITC-labelling casein to a similar level indicating they are proteolytically active.
evidence: Experimental data showing proteolytic activity of NETs from all five stimuli using FITC-casein assay (Figure 7B).

claim: NETs produced by all five stimuli are proteolytically active.
source: NETs from all five stimuli were capable of degrading FITC-labelling casein to a similar level indicating they are proteolytically active.
evidence: Experimental data showing proteolytic activity of NETs from all five stimuli using FITC-casein assay (Figure 7B).

claim: NETs produced by all five stimuli are capable of killing E. coli.
source: NETs produced by all five stimuli were capable of limited killing that was blocked in the presence of DNase 1 (Figure 7C).
evidence: Experimental data showing E. coli killing by NETs from all five stimuli (Figure 7C).

claim: The killing of E. coli by NETs is blocked in the presence of DNase 1.
source: NETs produced by all five stimuli were capable of limited killing that was blocked in the presence of DNase 1 (Figure 7C).
evidence: Experimental data showing loss of E. coli killing when NETs are degraded with DNase 1 (Figure 7C).

claim: NETs produced in response to PMA contain around 10% mitochondrial DNA.
source: NETs produced in response to PMA, nigericin, C. albicans and GBS contained around 10% mitochondrial DNA and A23187 NETs contained around 25% (Figure 7D).
evidence: Q-PCR data showing mitochondrial DNA content in PMA-induced NETs (Figure 7D).

claim: NETs produced in response to nigericin contain around 10% mitochondrial DNA.
source: NETs produced in response to PMA, nigericin, C. albicans and GBS contained around 10% mitochondrial DNA and A23187 NETs contained around 25% (Figure 7D).
evidence: Q-PCR data showing mitochondrial DNA content in nigericin-induced NETs (Figure 7D).

claim: NETs produced in response to C. albicans contain around 10% mitochondrial DNA.
source: NETs produced in response to PMA, nigericin, C. albicans and GBS contained around 10% mitochondrial DNA and A23187 NETs contained around 25% (Figure 7D).
evidence: Q-PCR data showing mitochondrial DNA content in C. albicans-induced NETs (Figure 7D).

claim: NETs produced in response to GBS contain around 10% mitochondrial DNA.
source: NETs produced in response to PMA, nigericin, C. albicans and GBS contained around 10% mitochondrial DNA and A23187 NETs contained around 25% (Figure 7D).
evidence: Q-PCR data showing mitochondrial DNA content in GBS-induced NETs (Figure 7D).

claim: NETs produced in response to A23187 contain around 25% mitochondrial DNA.
source: NETs produced in response to PMA, nigericin, C. albicans and GBS contained around 10% mitochondrial DNA and A23187 NETs contained around 25% (Figure 7D).
evidence: Q-PCR data showing mitochondrial DNA content in A23187-induced NETs (Figure 7D).

claim: NETs are mainly generated from chromosomal DNA.
source: This is in line with previous work demonstrating that NETs are mainly generated from chromosomal DNA (Lood et al., 2016).
evidence: Q-PCR data showing majority nuclear DNA content in NETs (Figure 7D), supported by citation to Lood et al., 2016.

claim: NETosis is not affected by caspase-3 inhibitor.
source: We treated neutrophils with a caspase-3 inhibitor to block apoptosis or necrostatin to prevent necroptosis and measured NET formation revealing that NETosis is not affected by either of these inhibitors (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: Experimental data showing no effect of caspase-3 inhibitor on NETosis induced by all five stimuli (Figure 8A-C).

claim: NETosis is not affected by necrostatin.
source: We treated neutrophils with a caspase-3 inhibitor to block apoptosis or necrostatin to prevent necroptosis and measured NET formation revealing that NETosis is not affected by either of these inhibitors (Figure 8A–C).
evidence: Experimental data showing no effect of necrostatin on NETosis induced by all five stimuli (Figure 8A-C).

claim: The apoptosis inducer staurosporine does not induce NET formation even after 6 hours incubation.
source: Importantly, the apoptosis inducer staurosporine did not induce NET formation even after 6 hr incubation (Figure 8D).
evidence: Experimental data showing no NET formation in response to staurosporine over 6 hours (Figure 8D).

claim: Staurosporine induces apoptosis in neutrophils as demonstrated by the presence of cleaved caspase-3.
source: As a control, we showed that staurosporine-induced apoptosis in neutrophils as demonstrated by the presence of cleaved caspase-3. This cleavage was blocked by a caspase-3 inhibitor (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Western blot data showing cleaved caspase-3 in response to staurosporine (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Staurosporine does not induce LDH release.
source: As expected, staurosporine did not induce LDH release (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Experimental data showing no LDH release in response to staurosporine (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Necrosis induced by α-hemolysin does not induce NETosis beyond the level seen in non-stimulated cells over a 6-hour time course.
source: Finally, we induced necrosis with α-hemolysin from Staphylococcus aureus or necroptosis with a cocktail of TNF-α, Z-VAD-FMK and a SMAC mimetic or cycloheximide (CHX) and measured NETosis. Neither necrosis nor necroptosis activation induced NETosis beyond the level seen in the non-stimulated cells over a 6-hr time course (Figure 8E).
evidence: Experimental data showing no NET formation in response to α-hemolysin over 6 hours (Figure 8E).

claim: Necroptosis induced by TNF-α, Z-VAD-FMK and a SMAC mimetic does not induce NETosis beyond the level seen in non-stimulated cells over a 6-hour time course.
source: Finally, we induced necrosis with α-hemolysin from Staphylococcus aureus or necroptosis with a cocktail of TNF-α, Z-VAD-FMK and a SMAC mimetic or cycloheximide (CHX) and measured NETosis. Neither necrosis nor necroptosis activation induced NETosis beyond the level seen in the non-stimulated cells over a 6-hr time course (Figure 8E).
evidence: Experimental data showing no NET formation in response to necroptosis inducers over 6 hours (Figure 8E).

claim: Necroptosis induced by TNF-α, Z-VAD-FMK and cycloheximide does not induce NETosis beyond the level seen in non-stimulated cells over a 6-hour time course.
source: Finally, we induced necrosis with α-hemolysin from Staphylococcus aureus or necroptosis with a cocktail of TNF-α, Z-VAD-FMK and a SMAC mimetic or cycloheximide (CHX) and measured NETosis. Neither necrosis nor necroptosis activation induced NETosis beyond the level seen in the non-stimulated cells over a 6-hr time course (Figure 8E).
evidence: Experimental data showing no NET formation in response to necroptosis inducers over 6 hours (Figure 8E).

claim: α-hemolysin induces cell death as measured by LDH release.
source: LDH assays confirmed that α-hemolysin and the necroptosis cocktail-induced cell death (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Experimental data showing LDH release in response to α-hemolysin (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).

claim: The necroptosis cocktail induces cell death as measured by LDH release.
source: LDH assays confirmed that α-hemolysin and the necroptosis cocktail-induced cell death (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Experimental data showing LDH release in response to necroptosis inducers (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Necrostatin blocks cell death due to necroptosis.
source: As a control, we verified that necrostatin blocked cell death due to necroptosis (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Experimental data showing inhibition of necroptosis-induced LDH release by necrostatin (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).

claim: PMA stimulation results in LDH release greater than non-stimulated cells at 4 hours.
source: Figure 8—figure supplement 1E showed that PMA, nigericin, C. albicans and GBS stimulation resulted in LDH release greater than non-stimulated cells at 4 hr.
evidence: Experimental data showing LDH release in response to PMA at 4 hours (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E).

claim: Nigericin stimulation results in LDH release greater than non-stimulated cells at 4 hours.
source: Figure 8—figure supplement 1E showed that PMA, nigericin, C. albicans and GBS stimulation resulted in LDH release greater than non-stimulated cells at 4 hr.
evidence: Experimental data showing LDH release in response to nigericin at 4 hours (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E).

claim: C. albicans stimulation results in LDH release greater than non-stimulated cells at 4 hours.
source: Figure 8—figure supplement 1E showed that PMA, nigericin, C. albicans and GBS stimulation resulted in LDH release greater than non-stimulated cells at 4 hr.
evidence: Experimental data showing LDH release in response to C. albicans at 4 hours (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E).

claim: GBS stimulation results in LDH release greater than non-stimulated cells at 4 hours.
source: Figure 8—figure supplement 1E showed that PMA, nigericin, C. albicans and GBS stimulation resulted in LDH release greater than non-stimulated cells at 4 hr.
evidence: Experimental data showing LDH release in response to GBS at 4 hours (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E).

claim: A23187 treatment results in LDH release but to a lesser extent than PMA, nigericin, C. albicans and GBS.
source: A23187 treatment also resulted in LDH release but to a lesser extent.
evidence: Experimental data showing LDH release in response to A23187 at 4 hours (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E).

claim: NETosis is a unique form of cell death that does not utilise components of the pathways associated with apoptosis, necrosis or necroptosis.
source: In conclusion, these data show that NETosis is a unique form of cell death that does not utilise components of the pathways associated with apoptosis, necrosis or necroptosis.
evidence: Summary of experimental data showing no effect of apoptosis, necrosis, or necroptosis inhibitors on NETosis and no NET formation by apoptosis, necrosis, or necroptosis inducers.

claim: PMA, C. albicans and GBS use a related pathway for NET induction.
source: We show that PMA, C. albicans and GBS use a related pathway for NET induction, whereas ionophores require an alternative pathway but that NETs produced by all stimuli are proteolytically active, kill bacteria and composed mainly of chromosomal DNA.
evidence: Summary of experimental data showing similar requirements (PKC, MPO, NE) for PMA, C. albicans, and GBS-induced NETosis.

claim: Ionophores require an alternative pathway for NET induction compared to PMA, C. albicans and GBS.
source: We show that PMA, C. albicans and GBS use a related pathway for NET induction, whereas ionophores require an alternative pathway but that NETs produced by all stimuli are proteolytically active, kill bacteria and composed mainly of chromosomal DNA.
evidence: Summary of experimental data showing different requirements (no PKC, ROS, MPO, or NE) for ionophore-induced NETosis.

claim: NETs produced by all stimuli are proteolytically active.
source: We show that PMA, C. albicans and GBS use a related pathway for NET induction, whereas ionophores require an alternative pathway but that NETs produced by all stimuli are proteolytically active, kill bacteria and composed mainly of chromosomal DNA.
evidence: Experimental data showing proteolytic activity of NETs from all five stimuli (Figure 7B).

claim: NETs produced by all stimuli kill bacteria.
source: We show that PMA, C. albicans and GBS use a related pathway for NET induction, whereas ionophores require an alternative pathway but that NETs produced by all stimuli are proteolytically active, kill bacteria and composed mainly of chromosomal DNA.
evidence: Experimental data showing E. coli killing by NETs from all five stimuli (Figure 7C).

claim: NETs produced by all stimuli are composed mainly of chromosomal DNA.
source: We show that PMA, C. albicans and GBS use a related pathway for NET induction, whereas ionophores require an alternative pathway but that NETs produced by all stimuli are proteolytically active, kill bacteria and composed mainly of chromosomal DNA.
evidence: Q-PCR data showing majority nuclear DNA content in NETs from all five stimuli (Figure 7D).

claim: NETosis occurs through several signalling mechanisms.
source: Thus, we demonstrate that NETosis occurs through several signalling mechanisms, suggesting that extrusion of NETs is important in host defence.
evidence: Summary of experimental data showing different pathway requirements for different stimuli.

claim: Extrusion of NETs is important in host defence.
source: Thus, we demonstrate that NETosis occurs through several signalling mechanisms, suggesting that extrusion of NETs is important in host defence.
evidence: Inference based on the existence of multiple pathways leading to NET formation.

claim: Neutrophils are the most abundant white blood cell in the circulation.
source: Neutrophils are the most abundant white blood cell in the circulation and serve as the first line of host defence against pathogen attack.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about neutrophils.

claim: Neutrophils serve as the first line of host defence against pathogen attack.
source: Neutrophils are the most abundant white blood cell in the circulation and serve as the first line of host defence against pathogen attack.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about neutrophils.

claim: Neutrophils are terminally differentiated, short lived cells that emerge from the bone marrow ready to react to the presence of pathogens.
source: They are terminally differentiated, short lived cells that emerge from the bone marrow ready to react to the presence of pathogens (Amulic et al., 2012; Kolaczkowska and Kubes, 2013).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about neutrophils, supported by citations to Amulic et al., 2012 and Kolaczkowska and Kubes, 2013.

claim: Neutrophils can phagocytose, degranulate and produce reactive oxygen species.
source: These include the ability to phagocytose, degranulate and produce reactive oxygen species (ROS).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about neutrophil functions.

claim: Neutrophils can produce chemokines and cytokines to alert other cells to danger.
source: The neutrophil can also produce chemokines and cytokines to alert other cells in the vicinity to the danger and thus maximise the host's immune response (Scapini and Cassatella, 2014).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about neutrophil functions, supported by citation to Scapini and Cassatella, 2014.

claim: Neutrophils release decondensed chromatin decorated with antimicrobial peptides that can capture pathogens in a process termed neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation.
source: Another form of defence utilised by the neutrophil is the release of decondensed chromatin decorated with antimicrobial peptides that can capture the pathogen in a process termed neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation (Brinkmann et al., 2004).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about NETs, supported by citation to Brinkmann et al., 2004.

claim: PMA is a potent mitogen and a robust NET inducer.
source: NETosis has been primarily examined in response to phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA), a potent mitogen and a robust NET inducer.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about PMA.

claim: PMA activates protein kinase C (PKC).
source: Neutrophils also initiate NETosis in response to microbial infections and, similarly to PMA, these activate protein kinase C (PKC), which in turn leads to calcium fluxes within the cell and activation of the NADPH oxidase signalling cascade resulting in the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Hakkim et al., 2011; Kaplan and Radic, 2012).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about PMA mechanism, supported by citations to Hakkim et al., 2011 and Kaplan and Radic, 2012.

claim: PKC activation leads to calcium fluxes within the cell.
source: Neutrophils also initiate NETosis in response to microbial infections and, similarly to PMA, these activate protein kinase C (PKC), which in turn leads to calcium fluxes within the cell and activation of the NADPH oxidase signalling cascade resulting in the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Hakkim et al., 2011; Kaplan and Radic, 2012).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about PKC signaling, supported by citations to Hakkim et al., 2011 and Kaplan and Radic, 2012.

claim: PKC activation leads to activation of the NADPH oxidase signalling cascade resulting in the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source: Neutrophils also initiate NETosis in response to microbial infections and, similarly to PMA, these activate protein kinase C (PKC), which in turn leads to calcium fluxes within the cell and activation of the NADPH oxidase signalling cascade resulting in the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Hakkim et al., 2011; Kaplan and Radic, 2012).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about PKC signaling, supported by citations to Hakkim et al., 2011 and Kaplan and Radic, 2012.

claim: Hydrogen peroxide produced during NETosis is consumed by myeloperoxidase (MPO) to produce hypochlorous acid and other oxidants.
source: The hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) produced is in turn consumed by myeloperoxidase (MPO) to produce hypochlorous acid as well as other oxidants (Papayannopoulos et al., 2010).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about MPO function in NETosis, supported by citation to Papayannopoulos et al., 2010.

claim: The production of ROS is responsible for the activation of the azurosome.
source: The production of ROS is responsible for the activation of the azurosome, a protein complex composed of MPO, the serine protease neutrophil elastase (NE) and cathepsin G among other granular proteins.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about azurosome activation.

claim: The generation of oxidants by MPO liberates neutrophil elastase from the azurosome.
source: The generation of oxidants by MPO liberates NE from the azurosome, allowing it to translocate to the nucleus where it aids in the decondensation of the chromatin by proteolyzing histones (Metzler et al., 2014).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about NE liberation, supported by citation to Metzler et al., 2014.

claim: Neutrophil elastase translocates to the nucleus where it aids in the decondensation of chromatin by proteolyzing histones.
source: The generation of oxidants by MPO liberates NE from the azurosome, allowing it to translocate to the nucleus where it aids in the decondensation of the chromatin by proteolyzing histones (Metzler et al., 2014).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about NE function in NETosis, supported by citation to Metzler et al., 2014.

claim: The cytoplasmic milieu mixes with the nuclear material as the nuclear and subsequently the plasma membrane break down, resulting in release of the NET.
source: Finally, the cytoplasmic milieu mixes with the nuclear material as the nuclear and subsequently the plasma membrane break down, resulting in release of the NET.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about NET release mechanism.

claim: CGD patients have mutations in genes coding for subunits of the NADPH oxidase complex.
source: To study the role of ROS in NETosis, we tested neutrophils isolated from chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) patients. These patients have mutations in genes coding for subunits of the NADPH oxidase complex and as such their neutrophils cannot make ROS (Heyworth et al., 2003).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about CGD, supported by citation to Heyworth et al., 2003.

claim: CGD patient neutrophils cannot make ROS.
source: These patients have mutations in genes coding for subunits of the NADPH oxidase complex and as such their neutrophils cannot make ROS (Heyworth et al., 2003).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about CGD, supported by citation to Heyworth et al., 2003.

claim: CGD patients are highly susceptible to bacterial and fungal infections.
source: Thus, these patients are highly susceptible to bacterial and fungal infections.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about CGD clinical phenotype.

claim: Citrullination is a post-transcriptional modification resulting in the conversion of arginine to citrulline.
source: Citrullination is a post-transcriptional modification resulting in the conversion of arginine to citrulline and is catalysed by a group of calcium-dependent proteins known as peptidylarginine deiminases (PADs) (Fuhrmann et al., 2015).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about citrullination, supported by citation to Fuhrmann et al., 2015.

claim: Citrullination is catalysed by peptidylarginine deiminases (PADs).
source: Citrullination is a post-transcriptional modification resulting in the conversion of arginine to citrulline and is catalysed by a group of calcium-dependent proteins known as peptidylarginine deiminases (PADs) (Fuhrmann et al., 2015).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about citrullination, supported by citation to Fuhrmann et al., 2015.

claim: Citrullination occurs during NETosis.
source: Recent studies have shown that citrullination occurs during NETosis (Lewis et al., 2015).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about citrullination in NETosis, supported by citation to Lewis et al., 2015.

claim: A23187 is a calcium ionophore produced during the growth of Streptomyces chartreusensis.
source: We selected five representative and well-described NET inducers that are effective over a 2.5–4 hr time period: (1) PMA, (2) the calcium ionophore A23187 which is produced during the growth of Streptomyces chartreusensis, (3) the potassium ionophore nigericin which is derived from the bacteria Streptomyces hygroscopicus, (4) Candida albicans hyphae and (5) Streptococcus agalactiae or Group B streptococcus (GBS) and examined NETosis (Figure 1A).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about A23187.

claim: Nigericin is a potassium ionophore derived from the bacteria Streptomyces hygroscopicus.
source: We selected five representative and well-described NET inducers that are effective over a 2.5–4 hr time period: (1) PMA, (2) the calcium ionophore A23187 which is produced during the growth of Streptomyces chartreusensis, (3) the potassium ionophore nigericin which is derived from the bacteria Streptomyces hygroscopicus, (4) Candida albicans hyphae and (5) Streptococcus agalactiae or Group B streptococcus (GBS) and examined NETosis (Figure 1A).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about nigericin.

claim: Patients with CGD suffer more frequently from invasive infections with A. fumigatus than with C. albicans.
source: These results are very much in line with the clinical phenotype in which patients with CGD suffer more frequently from invasive infections with A. fumigatus than with C. albicans (Henriet et al., 2012).
evidence: Established clinical knowledge about CGD, supported by citation to Henriet et al., 2012.

claim: CGD patient neutrophils produce significantly less NETs in response to A. fumigatus than healthy neutrophils.
source: Recently, a study demonstrated that CGD patient neutrophils produce significantly less NETs in response to A. fumigatus than healthy neutrophils further adding to our evidence that neutrophils from CGD patients react diversely to fungal infections (Gazendam et al., 2016).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge, supported by citation to Gazendam et al., 2016.

claim: Leishmania amazonensis can induce NETosis in the absence of ROS production.
source: Indeed, Leishmania amazonensis can induce NETosis in the absence of ROS production (Rochael et al., 2015; DeSouza-Vieira et al., 2016).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge, supported by citations to Rochael et al., 2015 and DeSouza-Vieira et al., 2016.

claim: Mitochondria can be a source of ROS in NETosis in response to calcium ionophores.
source: The role of ROS production in the generation of NETs is further confounded by recent work demonstrating that the mitochondria can also be a source of ROS in NETosis in response to calcium ionophores (Douda et al., 2015) or ribonucleoprotein-containing immune complexes (RNP ICs) (Lood et al., 2016).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge, supported by citation to Douda et al., 2015.

claim: Mitochondria can be a source of ROS in NETosis in response to ribonucleoprotein-containing immune complexes.
source: The role of ROS production in the generation of NETs is further confounded by recent work demonstrating that the mitochondria can also be a source of ROS in NETosis in response to calcium ionophores (Douda et al., 2015) or ribonucleoprotein-containing immune complexes (RNP ICs) (Lood et al., 2016).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge, supported by citation to Lood et al., 2016.

claim: Nigericin stimulates potassium effluxes in cells which results in the influx of calcium.
source: A23187 is a calcium ionophore that causes a massive influx of calcium and nigericin stimulates potassium effluxes in cells which also results in the influx of calcium demonstrating the similarity between the ionophores in their mechanism of NET induction (Yaron et al., 2015).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about nigericin mechanism, supported by citation to Yaron et al., 2015.

claim: Auto-antibodies directed against citrullinated proteins are commonly found in the serum of rheumatoid arthritis patients.
source: Auto-antibodies directed against citrullinated proteins are commonly found in the serum of rheumatoid arthritis patients (van Venrooij et al., 2004) and as such elucidating the origin of these modified proteins is of great therapeutic interest.
evidence: Established clinical knowledge, supported by citation to van Venrooij et al., 2004.

claim: PAD4-deficient mice do not generate NETs in response to a calcium ionophore.
source: Consistent with this, PAD4-deficient mice do not generate NETs in response to a calcium ionophore which is in direct contrast to the data presented here (Martinod et al., 2013).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge from mouse studies, supported by citation to Martinod et al., 2013.

claim: PAD inhibitors show efficacy in multiple mouse models of SLE and RA.
source: One additional discrepancy between our data and published reports is the observation that PAD inhibitors (both selective and pan-PAD) show efficacy in multiple mouse models of SLE and RA (Knight et al., 2015; Ghari et al., 2016; Kawalkowska et al., 2016).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge from mouse studies, supported by citations to Knight et al., 2015, Ghari et al., 2016, and Kawalkowska et al., 2016.

claim: Chromatin release as a form of host defence has been identified in both the animal and plant kingdoms.
source: Our observations show that there are different paths to NETosis in human cells. The elucidation of these pathways is of importance due to the ancient nature of chromatin release as a form of host defence as has been identified in both the animal and plant kingdoms. Therefore, it is unsurprising that NETosis is induced through a wide range of pathways (Tran et al., 2016).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge, supported by citation to Tran et al., 2016.

claim: NETs are present in the sputum of cystic fibrosis (CF) patients and contribute to the viscosity of the sputum.
source: NETs are present in the sputum of cystic fibrosis (CF) patients and contribute to the viscosity of the sputum (Manzenreiter et al., 2012).
evidence: Established clinical knowledge, supported by citation to Manzenreiter et al., 2012.

claim: NETs are evident in the thrombus in deep vein thrombosis (DVT).
source: NETs are evident in the thrombus in deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and disease activity is reflective of NET markers in the plasma (Fuchs et al., 2012).
evidence: Established clinical knowledge, supported by citation to Fuchs et al., 2012.

claim: Disease activity in deep vein thrombosis is reflective of NET markers in the plasma.
source: NETs are evident in the thrombus in deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and disease activity is reflective of NET markers in the plasma (Fuchs et al., 2012).
evidence: Established clinical knowledge, supported by citation to Fuchs et al., 2012.

claim: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) shows a very strong NET phenotype with regard to the presence of autoantibodies against proteins readily released from neutrophils in the process of NETosis.
source: Many autoimmune diseases such as Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and vasculitis also show a very strong NET phenotype with regard the presence of autoantibodies against proteins readily released from neutrophils in the process of NETosis such as anti-dsDNA and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic autoantibodies (Hakkim et al., 2010; Kessenbrock et al., 2009).
evidence: Established clinical knowledge, supported by citations to Hakkim et al., 2010 and Kessenbrock et al., 2009.

claim: Vasculitis shows a very strong NET phenotype with regard to the presence of autoantibodies against proteins readily released from neutrophils in the process of NETosis.
source: Many autoimmune diseases such as Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and vasculitis also show a very strong NET phenotype with regard the presence of autoantibodies against proteins readily released from neutrophils in the process of NETosis such as anti-dsDNA and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic autoantibodies (Hakkim et al., 2010; Kessenbrock et al., 2009).
evidence: Established clinical knowledge, supported by citations to Hakkim et al., 2010 and Kessenbrock et al., 2009.
